Where is the force transferred to the soil in a ground anchor?
Along the fixed (grouted) length, beyond the active slip surface
Uniformly along the whole length of the anchor
The free length runs in a sheath, no force is transferred; the fixed length extends beyond the active slip surface.
What are the typical inclination and maximum length of ground anchors?
They are made at an inclination of 15–30° to the horizontal, at most 25–30 m long; the fixed length is 4–9 m.
Why is the shortest anchor length 8 m?
Because both the free and the grouted length are at least 4 m
Because that is the length of the drill pipe
Because grouting is not possible below 8 m
Because the neighbouring plot is 8 m away
Both the free and the grouted length are at least 4 m, so the shortest anchor length is 8 m.
After how long a hardening period, and to what force, is the anchor prestressed?
After 8–12 days, to 80–90% of the design load
immediately, to 150% of the design force
after 1 day, to 20% of the design force
After hardening (8–12 days) the strands are prestressed through the head to 80–90% of the design load, then locked at the anchor head; a test load record is made for every anchor.
When is the use of steel tubular struts typically economical?
If anchors cannot be installed, or in a very deep excavation (over 15–20 m) where the movement of neighbouring buildings has to be limited
For every excavation shallower than 3 m
If the excavation is very wide (over 100 m)
If anchors cannot be installed because of the soil or neighbouring underground spaces, or for an excavation deeper than 15–20 m, where a stiff enough wall could not be built with anchors.
What becomes governing for tubular struts longer than 10–15 m?
The axial compressive force from thermal expansion
The deflection from the self-weight of the tube – nothing else
A strut warming up in the sun would expand, but squeezed between the walls it cannot – it has to be designed for the additional force.
What is the essence of the top-down (Milan) method?
After the walls and columns, the top slab is built first, and the further levels are excavated under the slab
First the whole excavation is dug, then construction proceeds from the bottom up
The slabs are lifted into place by crane
The excavation is secured by freezing
The top slab is cast on ground formwork and supports the walls as a diaphragm; the further levels are built under the slab by mining methods.
Where should the anchor wall of a passive tieback be placed?
Outside the active sliding wedge of the main wall, so that its passive wedge does not overlap the active wedge of the main wall
Right behind the main wall, 0,5 m away
In the middle of the excavation
It does not matter, as long as it is deep enough
It has to be outside the failure plane; if it stands inside the moving soil wedge, it moves together with the soil and gives no resistance.

Reinforcing bar, steel tube or steel nails are driven or vibrated into the ground – or fired with a compressed-air “gun”: no drilling, no spoil. Where possible, this is the most common method. The ballistic nail launcher fires a bar about 6 m long and 38–40 mm thick into the slope at ~350–400 km/h.

A Ø20–28 mm reinforcing bar is placed with centralisers (spacers) in a pre-drilled bore (typically Ø100–150 mm), which is then filled with cement grout from the bottom up. This is the solution in hard, stony clay and softer rock.

A variant of the drilled and grouted nail: a threaded hollow steel bar with a sacrificial drill bit. During drilling, flushing goes through the bar, and at the end grouting is done through it too – in one pass, without casing, even in collapsible soil.
The nail is installed with a high-pressure grout jet: the jet loosens the soil and forms the grout body around it.
A steel shaft with helical plates or a thread, driven in by rotation – without grouting. Rarer in practice.
